introduction_markdown: Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board, General Certificate of Education Examination, June 2020, Ordinary Level, Physics, Paper 2 (subject code 0580). Time allowed: two and a half hours. Answer ALL questions. Section I is designed to be answered in 1 hour and Section II in 1 1/2 hours. You are advised to divide your time accordingly. In Section II answer EITHER the a, b and c OR the d, e and f of each question. For your guidance the approximate mark for each part of a question is indicated in brackets. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. In calculations you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. Where necessary, assume: the acceleration of free fall, $g = 10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$; the speed of light in air, $c = 3\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the charge on an electron, $e = 1.6\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$. Calculators are allowed.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**EITHER 7 (a), (b) and (c)**

(i) State two reasons why some solids float in water, while others sink in water. *[2 marks]*

(ii) Describe an experiment to determine the density of a piece of iron. Your account should include: an experimental setup or a list of the required apparatus; the procedure to follow; the measurements to be made; how to obtain a conclusion from the measurements; any precaution taken. *[6 marks]*

(iii) Name one use of a solid with: a high density; a low density. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) 1. A solid **floats** if its density is **less than** the density of water, and **sinks** if its density is **greater than** that of water.
2. A floating solid displaces a weight of water equal to its own weight (the upthrust equals its weight); a sinking solid is heavier than the largest upthrust the water can give. (The shape also matters: a hollow object such as a ship contains air, so its average density is less than that of water.)

(ii) **Apparatus:** electronic balance, measuring cylinder, water, thin thread, small piece of iron that fits in the cylinder.

**Set-up:** the iron is tied to a thread and lowered into a measuring cylinder containing some water; the water level rises by the volume of the iron (displacement method).

**Procedure:** 1. Weigh the piece of iron on the balance and record its mass $m$. 2. Half fill the measuring cylinder with water and read the volume $V_1$. 3. Tie the iron to the thread and lower it gently until it is completely under water; read the new volume $V_2$.

**Measurements:** mass $m$ of the iron, initial volume $V_1$ and final volume $V_2$.

**Conclusion:** the volume of the iron is $V = V_2 - V_1$, so its density is $\rho = \dfrac{m}{V_2 - V_1}$ (in $\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$ or, after conversion, $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$). Iron gives about $7.9\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$. Repeating the experiment and averaging improves the result.

**Precautions:** read the water level at eye level at the bottom of the meniscus; lower the iron gently to avoid splashing; make sure no air bubbles cling to it and that it is fully submerged; dry the iron before weighing.

(iii) **High density:** lead used in the keel (ballast) of ships, as fishing sinkers or as radiation shielding. **Low density:** cork or foam used in life jackets and floats (or aluminium used for aircraft bodies; helium in balloons).

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 4 shows a bob suspended on a rubber band such that the system is stable.

![fig-1](gce-ol-physics-2020-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_7_fig_1.png)

(i) Copy the diagram and show two forces acting on the system. *[2 marks]*

(ii) Name the forms of energy possessed by the rubber band and the bob. *[2 marks]*

(iii) Do all elastic materials obey Hooke's law? Justify with examples. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) Copy the support, the rubber band and the bob. Draw two arrows on the bob: the **weight $W$ of the bob acting vertically downwards** and the **tension $T$ in the rubber band acting vertically upwards**. Since the system is stable (at rest), $T = W$. *(The drawing is made by the candidate.)*

(ii) The **rubber band** has **elastic (strain) potential energy** because it is stretched. The **bob** has **gravitational potential energy** because it is above the ground (it has no kinetic energy because it is at rest).

(iii) **No.** Hooke's law (extension proportional to the force) is obeyed only up to the limit of proportionality. A steel spring or a metal wire obeys it within this limit, but a rubber band is elastic and does **not** obey Hooke's law (its force-extension graph is a curve, not a straight line). Even a spring stops obeying the law when overstretched beyond its limit of proportionality.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 5 shows the velocity-time graph of a car which starts from rest and moves for 20 seconds.

![fig-2](gce-ol-physics-2020-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_7_fig_2.png)

(i) Describe the motion of the car in section OA and section AB of the graph. *[2 marks]*

(ii) Calculate the distance covered by the car from rest for the 20 seconds. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) **OA:** the velocity increases steadily from $0$ to $5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in $10\,\mathrm{s}$: the car moves with **constant (uniform) acceleration** $a = \dfrac{5-0}{10} = 0.5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

**AB:** the velocity stays at $5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ from $10\,\mathrm{s}$ to $20\,\mathrm{s}$: the car moves with **constant (uniform) velocity** (zero acceleration).

(ii) Distance = area under the graph:

Triangle OA: $\dfrac{1}{2}\times 10\times 5 = 25\,\mathrm{m}$.

Rectangle under AB: $10\times 5 = 50\,\mathrm{m}$.

Total distance $= 25 + 50 = 75\,\mathrm{m}$.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**OR 7 (d), (e) and (f)**

(i) State two ways by which waves are classified. *[2 marks]*

(ii) Describe an experiment to show that light does not need a material medium for propagation, but that sound needs a material medium for propagation. Your description should include: an experimental setup or a list of required apparatus; the procedure to follow; the measurements or observations made; how to obtain a conclusion from the observations; any precaution taken. *[6 marks]*

(iii) State one practical situation each in which a wave is used because it either needs a material medium to travel or it does not need a material medium to travel. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) 1. By the **direction of vibration** compared with the direction of travel: **transverse** waves (e.g. light, water waves) and **longitudinal** waves (e.g. sound).
2. By whether they **need a medium**: **mechanical** waves (need a material medium, e.g. sound) and **electromagnetic** waves (do not need a medium, e.g. light, radio waves).

(ii) **Apparatus:** electric bell, bell jar on a base plate with an airtight seal, vacuum pump and tube, battery and switch, connecting wires, soft support (foam or thread) for the bell.

**Set-up:** the electric bell is hung by thread (or placed on foam) inside the bell jar, with its wires passing through the seal to the battery and switch. The bell jar is connected to the vacuum pump.

**Procedure:** 1. Switch on the bell and note that it can be heard and seen. 2. Start the vacuum pump and slowly remove the air from the jar. 3. Keep watching the bell and listening. 4. Then let the air back in.

**Observations:** as air is removed the sound becomes fainter and fainter until it is almost inaudible, although the hammer of the bell can still be seen vibrating through the glass. When the air is let back in the sound becomes loud again.

**Conclusion:** light still reaches the eye from the bell through the vacuum, so light does **not** need a material medium. Sound fades when the air is removed, so sound **needs** a material medium (air) to travel.

**Precautions:** support the bell on foam or thread so that sound is not conducted through the base plate; make sure the seal is airtight; remove the air slowly and completely; do not touch the jar.

(iii) **Needs a medium:** sound waves are used in ultrasound scanning (or sonar to find the depth of the sea, or speech and music over air). **Does not need a medium:** light from the Sun reaches the Earth through space, and radio waves are used to carry signals between satellites and the ground (television, mobile phones).

Figure 6 shows a convex lens, L, of focal length $5\,\mathrm{cm}$, with an object, O, placed perpendicularly to its principal axis.

![fig-3](gce-ol-physics-2020-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_7_fig_3.png)

(i) Copy the diagram and use any two rays of light from the object to indicate how the lens forms an image of the object. *[3 marks]*

(ii) Give any two characteristics of the image formed. *[2 marks]*

(iii) Name a practical device in which a lens is used to form an image of an object as in Figure 6. *[1 mark]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) The object is about $7.5\,\mathrm{cm}$ from the lens, that is **between $F$ ($5\,\mathrm{cm}$) and $2F$ ($10\,\mathrm{cm}$)**. Copy the diagram, then draw from the top of the object: **ray 1**, parallel to the principal axis, which is refracted by the lens so as to **pass through the principal focus on the other side**; **ray 2**, through the optical centre of the lens, which goes straight on **without deviation**. The two refracted rays cross on the far side of the lens, beyond $2F$ (at about $15\,\mathrm{cm}$ from the lens, using $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{5} - \dfrac{1}{7.5}$ so $v = 15\,\mathrm{cm}$). The image is drawn as an arrow from the axis to the crossing point, pointing downwards. *(The drawing is made by the candidate.)*

(ii) The image is **real**, **inverted** (upside down) and **magnified** (larger than the object).

(iii) A **projector** (slide, film or cinema projector).

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 7 shows a thin metal wire, AB, which is tied at the points A and B such that it is stiff.

![fig-4](gce-ol-physics-2020-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_7_fig_4.png)

(i) Name the energy changes which take place if the wire is plucked with the finger or a small piece of broom. *[2 marks]*

(ii) Sketch a diagram to show the appearance of the plucked wire, and indicate the distance that represents one wavelength. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) Chemical energy in the muscles is changed to **kinetic energy** of the finger; this gives **elastic (strain) potential energy** to the wire as it is pulled sideways. When released, the potential energy changes to the **kinetic energy** of the vibrating wire (the two forms change into each other as the wire vibrates). The vibrating wire sets the air in motion, so part of the energy becomes **sound energy** (and a little heat).

(ii) The wire is fixed at A and B, so these ends cannot move (they are nodes). Plucked in the middle, the wire vibrates in a single loop: draw the wire as a smooth curved arch bulging between A and B (with the dotted position on the other side of the line AB). This single loop is **half a wavelength**, so **one wavelength $\lambda = 2\times AB$**: show it by continuing the curve as a dotted second loop below AB and marking $\lambda$ over the length of the two loops. (If the wire is plucked at one quarter of its length it vibrates in two loops, and then one wavelength is equal to the whole distance AB.) *(The drawing is made by the candidate.)*
